summary: Five Sides is a browser instrument that plays NASA Earth Information Center animations as music. Eighteen scenes are taken from each animation, measured pixel by pixel, and played one per bar, so the same data arrives through the eyes and the ears at the same instant and the picture keeps moving inside the bar rather than sitting still behind it. It ships five records, city lights, atmospheric carbon dioxide, forest canopy height, lightning seen from the International Space Station, and sea surface temperature, plus a live tuner that builds a new side from the last eighteen days of NASA imagery. Every sound is generated in the page from a measurement of the pixels; every bar can describe itself in words for listeners who cannot see it. Built for blind and low-vision listeners first, and for everyone else.
details:
Team One Man vs All (solo entry; Local Event: Manila, Philippines). Challenge: The Earth Information Jukebox.

What it does and how it works?

Five Sides is a single-page web application, running entirely in the browser, that turns NASA Earth Information Center animations into music. Eighteen scenes are cut from each published animation and measured pixel by pixel: luminance, saturation, a circular-mean hue, Hasler–Süsstrunk colourfulness, position along the record's own published colour bar, gradient texture, and activity across sixteen columns and six bands — roughly 230,000 samples per frame in about eight milliseconds. Each scene becomes one bar. Brightness chooses the register, position on the colour bar chooses the scale degree, texture sets note density, and the change since the previous scene sets tempo. The browser decodes the animation and draws it into the page while the Web Audio API synthesises the music live, so the picture moves inside the bar rather than sitting still behind it. Five records ship with the page — City Lights, Carbon Weather, Canopy, Lightning, Ocean Heat — and a live tuner builds a new side from the last eighteen days of NASA GIBS imagery.

Benefits.

Every bar can describe itself in words, generated from the same numbers that produced the sound, and can be spoken aloud as it plays: the picture is optional, the description is not. The instrument is fully keyboard-operable, honours reduced motion, and carries a ‘Show NASA frame’ switch that removes every overlay so the raw data can be checked at any moment. Because the mapping is deterministic arithmetic rather than a model, the same scene always produces the same music and any note can be traced back to a measurement; nothing here can be hallucinated.

Intended impact.

Earth science is delivered almost entirely through sight, which excludes blind and low-vision readers before the first chart is drawn. Five Sides gives that audience the measurements in a modality that carries change over time better than a still image, and gives sighted audiences a fast way to feel the shape of a dataset — a classroom, a museum floor, or a newsroom meeting sea surface temperature for the first time. Nothing in the instrument is specific to one dataset, so the same approach can carry any EIC visual with a published colour bar.

Tools and technology.

HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript — no framework, no bundler, no build step — served as static files from Vercel behind a strict content security policy. Canvas 2D for pixel measurement and drawing; Web Audio API for synthesis, with OfflineAudioContext for WAV export. Python and FFmpeg cut scenes from the published NASA renditions and write the catalogue; Node runs 62 unit checks, and a headless Chromium driven over the DevTools Protocol runs 18 browser checks covering the accessibility tree, keyboard operation, export and reduced motion. Imagery comes from the NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (EIC Content Database) and NASA GIBS. Source and documentation: https://github.com/EngrAlegre/NASA_JUKEBOX

How it is creative?

The instrument treats the legend as the score. The colour bar the scientists drew to explain temperature or canopy height becomes the pitch axis, so the interface's own explanation is what a listener hears. Each bar is a scene rather than a still — the animation is slowed to the length of the bar — which makes the music a reading of movement rather than a description of a picture. And the piece is willing to be silent: where the satellite recorded nothing, the bar plays a rest instead of inventing sound.

What was considered?

Space is black, so an absolute brightness scale would trap every record in the bottom octave; each feature is calibrated within its own side by 10th and 90th percentile, with the raw value kept for display. Eighteen bars have to stay listenable, so pitches come from a fixed mode, tempo moves at most seven BPM per bar, and harmony walks one scale step per bar instead of leaping. Fidelity was preferred to prettiness: two rows of the mapping table are marked artistic rather than measured, the sample is described as eighteen scenes rather than the whole sequence, and the repository states plainly what has not been verified — no blind participant has tested it yet.
